newsitem.title: USA: LDC debt mixed, as spreads back off record highs.
newsitem.headline: LDC debt mixed, as spreads back off record highs.

text.p: Brady bond prices were mixed as spreads widened slightly against U.S. Treasuries, backing off their flirtation with new record levels, emerging market traders said.

The emerging debt market has clung to stunning tight levels for the past few weeks, watching the JP Morgan Emerging Market Bond Index-plus rise 3.7 percent in July, as players held onto their positions.
"Spreads are very tight and that's something we've got to live with until something corrects," said Peter Allen, director of emerging market research at BankBoston.
In sparce trade on Wednesday the overall EMBI index widened about one basis point to 373, dealers said.
The benchmark U.S. Treasury bond had a banner day, climbing 26/32 to yield 6.33 percent on technical factors.

"The long bond is the main driver of momentum in this market," said one Brady bond trader, noting that Wall Street dealers seemed reluctant to add to their hefty stockpiles of emerging debt. "I'm not really crazy about going short, but I wouldn't buy any more."
In the major Latin American issues, the liquid Brazil
"C" bond gained 3/8 to a bid price of 84 and Mexican pars edged up 1/4 to 82-3/8.

U.S. analysts looked to high yield paper to lead the market, as Ecuadorean Bradies stormed higher. Ecuador's PDIs tightened about nine basis points to 71-1/2, while the country's par bonds picked up around 12 basis points to 54-7/8.
"In the very short term the high yielders -- Ecuador Russia and Bulgaria -- will continue to outperform," said Carlos Asilis, Latin American strategist at UBS Securities.
"Credit conditions continued to be benevolent and global liquidity continues to be very positive," Asilis added.

The markets reacted warmly to the announcement late Tuesday that the Brazil government named Gustavo Franco to replace Gustavo Loyola as head of the central bank. Analysts said that Franco, an architect of the country's stabilization plan, would hold the line on foreign exchange policy.
"In my view it didn't amount to much because the market had been expecting the departure of Loyola for a long time," Asilis said.
BankBoston's Allen also expressed confidence in Franco: "He's now central bank president so he speaks with more authority. He may have more influence on non central bank issues," Allen said.
